screens.prompt: In E2, look up the salary for the ID in D2 using the table in A1:C6.

hints.syntax: Four arguments, in this order: the ID, the table A2:C6, the column number 3, and FALSE. =VLOOKUP(D2,A2:C6,3,FALSE).
hints.func-vlookup: VLOOKUP does the work here: the grader wants the function, not the number copied out of C5.
hints.exact-match: Add FALSE (or 0) as the fourth argument. Left out, Excel uses approximate match, which on this ID column returns a neighbouring employee's salary.
hints.require-ref: Point at D2 and at the table, so the answer moves when the payroll file moves.
hints.value: Right employee, wrong column: the salary is column 3 of A:C. Column 2 holds the name.
hints.error: #REF! means the column number runs past A:C, which has three columns. #N/A means the ID was not found; #VALUE! means the second argument is not a range.
hints.hardcoded: The answer only survives while Dee is on 54000, so the figure was typed in. Let VLOOKUP fetch it and a pay rise follows.

reject.why: no fourth argument, so Excel defaults to approximate
returns the name column, not the salary
the right lookup, the wrong employee
the table starts at B, so the ID column is gone
the salary is typed, not looked up
compares the salary against the typed 54,000, so a pay rise returns 0

variants.why: Dee goes from 54,000 to 54,100, so the lookup has to return the new salary

docs.explain:
VLOOKUP reads down the first column of a table until it finds the lookup value, then returns the cell in that row at the column number you name. The ID in D2 is E-104, which sits in row 5. Column 3 of that row holds 54000, so the formula =VLOOKUP(D2,A2:C6,3,FALSE) returns 54000.

The fourth argument decides the mode. FALSE, or 0, asks for an exact hit and gives #N/A when the ID is absent. TRUE, or nothing at all, matches approximately: it stops on the last row it passed, so an ID column can return another employee's salary without an error.

Write FALSE every time on an ID column. Left out, the match is the silent kind, and a wrong salary looks like a right one until payroll disagrees.

errors.text: The ID is missing from the first column, often because it carries a trailing space or is stored as a number rather than text.
The column number is wider than the table: 4 applied to A:C, which holds three columns.
The second argument is not a range of cells, or the column number is zero.

docs.atWork: Payroll runs, price lists and product feeds: two exports joined by a key, one of them read for a figure.
docs.outcome: Pull a salary out of a table by its ID, with the exact-match flag written out.

seo.title: VLOOKUP in Excel: exact match lookup
seo.description: VLOOKUP with FALSE finds an exact hit or #N/A, and TRUE guesses at the nearest row. The fourth argument decides whether the salary is right.
